listings.description_full: Rarely does a property come to market that combines this much land, water, infrastructure, and operating business in one package. This 572 acre property in Sevier County, Utah, just outside Richfield, is a complete, vertically integrated landscape materials operation with decades of production history, statewide customers, and multiple income streams already in place. Improvements and UtilitiesThe property is served by power and natural gas, with road access from multiple points and frontage on both State Route 118 and Interstate 70, an ideal setup for shipping and marketing. Improvements include a 7,500 square foot 7-bedroom, 5-bathroom home built in 1995, expanded in 2018, and a 5,000 square foot shop with three bays, auto lifts, air compressors, a built-in office, and ample storage, giving the operation a practical base for equipment maintenance, fleet work, parts, and administration. The Land and WaterThe property carries an exceptional water portfolio. Underground water rights include Water Right (WR) 63-4462, decreed for 5.82 CFS or 576.4 acres with a 1874 priority date, one of the earliest and most senior rights in the area. Secondary rights add further depth: WR 63-159 (1.54 acre-feet), WR 63-189 (4.48 acre-feet), and WR 63-4409 (0.25 acre-feet). Additional surface water is delivered through 289.28 shares of Sevier Valley Canal and 93 shares of Piute Class A stock water, all included in the sale. Irrigation water moves through an underground pipeline system with risers and control valves spread across the property, feeding a sprinkler mainline built around Yellowmine pipe and wheel lines, all of which convey with the sale. Together, this infrastructure supports efficient water delivery and flexible coverage across the entire acreage. Of the 572 total acres, more than 315 are currently dedicated to sod production and could transition easily to other agricultural uses. The ground is flat and buildable, with views of red rock hills to the north and open farmland in every direction, and the property has strong subdivision potential in several areas, along with ground already approved for a dry storage facility. The BusinessThis listing includes a complete, vertically integrated landscape materials business: Willowwood Turf / All American Sod and Super Soil USA (gravel, soil, and composting), along with their branded products, active websites, and existing customer base. For nearly 50 years, this operation has supplied drought-tolerant turf across Utah, grown in naturally occurring "Ferrozite," an iron-rich silt loam unique to the region that produces denser, darker-green, more resilient turf. Beyond turf, the operation runs a diversified materials business producing screened and enhanced soils, fine wood compost, and Super Soil blends, along with gravel, road base, and related aggregates, Ferrozite soil amendment, and "Strawberry Cream" decorative rock. On-site composting and blending operations turn local organic material into premium mixes that pair Ferrozite's mineral profile with organic matter. Additional ground within the parcels is well-suited for subdivision in a growing area, and separate ground is already approved for a dry storage facility, adding further upside beyond the existing operations. Each piece of this business- turf, soils and composting, and gravel- can run independently or as a single cohesive operation, giving a buyer flexibility to continue it as-is, scale one segment, or repurpose the ground for other agricultural or development uses. With decades of production history, statewide customers ranging from homeowners to municipalities, and established outlets and websites, this is a complete package with considerable upside. The property sits in a rural setting close to Richfield, with every convenience nearby, including gas stations, restaurants, a grocery store, a Walmart, a hospital, Snow College's Richfield campus, and the Sevier Valley Events Center. For years, the current owner has been pushing the envelope of what is possible for high-elevation hay. The focus has been on steadily increasing the quality feed value metrics while also reducing inputs such as fertilizer and pesticides. Forage output has been routinely tested through Dairy One Forage Testing, with results placing production in the high-quality category for: Dry Matter, Crude Protein, ADF, NDF, TDN, and feed value. Management practices have focused on soil health and microbiology, with reduced fertilizer inputs and limited use of pest control products. Hay handling infrastructure includes Staheli West steamers, covered storage, and dedicated hay barns designed to preserve forage quality during storage and transport. Through cutting-edge processes, including microbiology additives and a soil health focus, this farm runs incredibly efficiently, resulting in higher net margins and more efficient water usage. Speaking of water, the 370 acres in production are fed by 302 shares of the east bench, 111.5 shares of the long canal, and 81 shares of West Panguitch Irrigation. In addition to the water shares, the farm also has 180 ELUS and 1.6 homes of underground water rights, a total of over 15 ACFT of well-fed stock watering to go along with the 1.6 homes. With water being paramount in Utah, this farm has sufficient water resources to continue production even in severe drought years. Power infrastructure has been improved over the years as well by using a Variable Frequency Drive (VFD), providing increased power when needed, resulting in total yearly utility bills of just $16,000 for the entire operation. Construction of the home and heated shop was started shortly after the purchase in 2018. The custom home features numerous upgrades to go with 6 bedrooms, 3 full bathrooms, and 2 half bathrooms, including an outside-accessible farm hand washroom in over 3,400 square feet. Hay storage includes one three-sided barn over 10,000 square feet and three smaller covered hay storage areas near Highway 89, with an additional 10,000 square feet in covered storage. Next to the main home, 3,600 square feet of covered parking adjoin a 2,700 square foot heated shop with two large fuel tanks and a water storage/softener system for hay steamers. No details have been overlooked, and this farm runs effectively and efficiently. The main property is fully fenced and could also provide irrigated grazing pasture for up to 300 cow-calf pairs, with the additional acreage used to store hay for the winter months, creating a fully-functional year-round cow-calf operation without the need to utilize expensive and timely trucking between summer and winter range. While equipment is not included in the price, the seller is willing to negotiate and include the necessary equipment to continue effective production. Buyers are also encouraged to get soil testing completed upon purchase to obtain soil tax credits, where eligible. Strong water rights and sufficient water shares, new equipment, well-maintained and managed operations make this one of the premier hay farms in the mountain west.

The original sale area contains about 56 acres and is being divided into the following 3 tracts.,,The exact acreage will be determined by survey:,,TRACT ONE = 14 acres +/-,TRACT TWO = 28 acres +/-,TRACT THREE = 14 acres +/-,,MINERAL RESOURCES,The Marcellus Shale and Utica Shale are understood to underlie the property at a depth of 5000 feet+ and 10,000+ feet, respectively. The east coast Marcellus Shale Region is believed to contain enough natural gas to power the United States for over 100 years.,,The owner has not leased the oil and gas rights and all mineral rights the seller has in title will be transferred to the purchaser at closing. There are no known coal reserves underlying the property. All prospective purchasers are encouraged to have an attorney do a title search prior to purchasing.,,UTILITIES,Water: Public water may be available along Route 219,Sewer: Public Sewer may be available along Route 219,Electricity: On site,Telephone: Available along Route 219,Internet: May be Optimum or Verizon Cable. Starlink Satellite is available in the area,Cellphone Coverage: Excellent coverage with 5G,,ZONING,There is currently no county zoning in Monroe County. All prospective purchasers are encouraged to contact the Monroe County Health Department for answers regarding installation of septic systems and water wells. Further information on county zoning may be answered by contacting the Monroe County Commission.,,PUBLIC SCHOOLS,Monroe County School District,,Public Elementary School:,Mountain View Elementary School, Union,,Public Middle School:,Mountain View Middle School, Union,,Public High School:,James Monroe High School,Monroe County Vocational Center,,Monroe County Schools have had a graduation rate of 95% for the past several years indicating a stable educational environment.  The school districts revenue/student ratio is higher than the state median, and the spending/student ratio is also higher, suggesting a positive financial investment in education.,,The student/teacher ratio is higher than the West Virginia state average, which may indicate a focus on providing more resources to students.,,Overall, Monroe County Schools have a strong commitment to education, with a focus on providing a stable and supportive learning environment.,,AIRPORT ACCESS and REGIONAL CONNECTIVITY,The property is conveniently located within a two-hour drive of multiple regional and commercial airports, providing flexible travel options for landowners, visitors, and investors. This balance of rural seclusion with dependable infrastructure is a key reason the area continues to attract buyers from the Mid-Atlantic and Southeast.,,Highway & Ground Access,,Direct access via Interstate 64, Interstate 77, U.S. Route 219, and U.S. Route 19,Well maintained state highways provide reliable year-round access,Easy connections to:,,Charleston, WV,Lewisburg & the Greenbrier Valley,Virginia and North Carolina markets,Greenbrier Valley Airport (LWB) Lewisburg, WV,Approx. 1520 minutes,,Commercial passenger service with direct flights to Charlotte (CLT) and Chicago (ORD),Free parking, easy access, and a modern terminal make this a convenient local option,Roanoke Blacksburg Regional Airport (ROA) Roanoke, VA,Approx. 1 hour 40 minutes,,Larger regional airport offering multiple daily flights to major hubs,Full airline service, rental cars, and expanded scheduling,Beckley Raleigh County Memorial Airport (BKW) Beckley, WV,Approx. 1 hour,,Regional airport with scheduled commercial service,Easy access for southern West Virginia and regional travel,Yeager Airport (CRW) Charleston, WV,Approx. 2 hours,,West Virginias largest commercial airport,Broad selection of domestic flights and airline carriers,Charlottesville Albemarle Airport (CHO) Charlottesville, VA,Approx. 2 hours,,Popular regional airport serving central Virginia,Convenient for travelers connecting through the MidAtlantic region,,WILDLIFE & NATURAL FEATURES,The property offers excellent wildlife habitat and is home to a wide variety of native species. The acreage provides ideal cover, travel corridors, and natural forage, making it well suited for wildlife viewing and recreational use. Deer, turkey, and small game are commonly found throughout the property, along with a variety of songbirds and other native wildlife.,,The mix of open and wooded areas creates a diverse and balanced environment that supports year-round wildlife activity, offering a peaceful rural setting with frequent animal sightings.,,CARBON SEQUESTRATION,Carbon sequestration is the natural process by which forests, soils, and vegetation absorb and store carbon dioxide (CO) from the atmosphere, helping regulate climate and improve environmental health. Well managed land can act as a long-term carbon sink, storing carbon for decades or even centuries.,,In rural and forested regions, carbon sequestration is one of the most valuable and increasingly recognized ecosystem services land can provide.,,How Land Sequesters Carbon:,,Forests,Trees absorb CO through photosynthesis and store carbon in:,,Trunks and branches,Roots,Leaf litter and forest soils,Mature forests continue to store carbon while younger forests actively remove carbon from the air as they grow.,,Soils,,Healthy soils store large amounts of carbon below ground through:,,Root systems,Organic matter,Microbial activity,Undisturbed soils especially forest and pasture soils are highly effective at long term carbon storage.,,Natural Landscapes,,Wetlands, riparian buffers, and native grasslands also contribute significantly by slowing carbon release and stabilizing organic material.,,MONROE COUNTY'S KARST LANDSCAPE - GEOLOGICALLY EXTRAORDINARY,Monroe County sits atop a world-class karst landscape shaped by the Greenbrier Limestone, featuring some of the highest sinkhole densities, longest cave systems, and most complex groundwater flow in the Appalachian region and North America. This makes it geologically extraordinary.,,Karst landscapes are shaped by the gradual dissolution of soluble rocks like limestone, creating distinctive features such as caves, sinkholes, cliffs, and underground rivers. These landforms foster a wide range of habitats above and below ground, supporting diverse plant and animal life.,,Underground caves offer stable conditions for organisms adapted to low light and unique soil chemistry, including certain fish, amphibians, invertebrates, and bats. Surface areas with nutrient rich, calcium-based soils support a variety of plants, mosses, ferns, and forests, which in turn provide habitats for birds and terrestrial animals.,,Karst landscapes combine extraordinary natural, geological, ecological, and cultural values, representing unique ecosystems and human history over millennia.,,ANCIENT TREES,Ancient trees on West Virginia farms such as white oaks, tulip poplars, hickories, sycamores, and beeches are living links to the region's deep history. Many predate European settlement and were preserved when land was cleared for agriculture, becoming integral parts of farm landscapes. Beyond offering shade and landmarks, these trees support wildlife, stabilize soil, and store carbon. Today, they are often cherished as family heirlooms and increasingly recognized for their ecological and cultural value, symbolizing the long relationship between people and Appalachia's land.,,ABOUT MONROE COUNTY, WEST VIRGINIA,Monroe County is located in southeastern West Virginia, along the Virginia border, and is known for its scenic mountain landscapes, rolling farmland, and strong agricultural heritage. The county offers a peaceful rural setting with wide open spaces, low population density, and a slower pace of life that appeals to landowners, outdoor enthusiasts, and those seeking privacy.,,The area is characterized by forested ridges, fertile valleys, and clear streams, creating an ideal environment for farming, recreation, and wildlife habitat. Monroe County is especially attractive to buyers interested in hunting, hiking, livestock, homesteading, or recreational land use.,,The county seat, Union, provides essential services, smalltown charm, and local businesses, while larger towns and amenities are accessible within reasonable driving distance. Monroe County maintains a strong sense of community while preserving its rural character.,,With its combination of natural beauty, accessible location, and traditional Appalachian landscape, Monroe County continues to be a desirable area for land ownership, investment, and rural living.,,NEIGHBORING GREENBRIER COUNTY, WEST VIRGINIA,Greenbrier County offers a wide variety of natural, historic, and recreational attractions, making it a highly desirable area for outdoor enthusiasts and those seeking a scenic Appalachian lifestyle.,,The county is well known for outdoor recreation, including hiking, biking, hunting, fishing, and horseback riding. Miles of country roads, forested ridges, and river valleys provide year-round opportunities to enjoy the outdoors. Nearby rivers and streams support trout fishing, kayaking, and other water activities.,,Lewisburg, the county seat, is a nationally recognized historic town featuring locally owned shops, restaurants, galleries, and cultural events. The area blends historic charm with modern conveniences, making it a regional destination for dining, arts, and entertainment.,,Greenbrier County is also home to The Greenbrier, a world-famous historic resort known for its architecture, golf courses, spa, and rich history. The presence of this landmark contributes to the areas visibility and tourism while preserving the county's rural character.,,Nearby parks, caverns, and scenic overlooks including state parks and natural areas offer additional opportunities for exploration and outdoor recreation. Seasonal events, festivals, and agricultural fairs further highlight the county's strong community and cultural traditions.,,With its combination of natural beauty, outdoor activities, historic destinations, and smalltown attractions, Greenbrier County continues to be a sought after area for visitors and landowners alike.,,OUTDOOR & RECREATIONAL OPPORTUNITIES IN WEST VIRGINIA,West Virginia known as The Mountain State offers some of the most diverse and accessible outdoor recreation in the eastern United States. With rugged mountains, deep forests, and free flowing rivers, the state is a destination for both adventure seekers and nature focused property owners.,,Hiking, Trail Systems & Scenic Overlooks,West Virginia features hundreds of miles of hiking and biking trails, ranging from gentle forest walks to challenging ridge and gorge routes. Popular areas include the Monongahela National Forest, state parks, rail trails, and scenic overlooks with long range mountain views. Fall foliage hiking is especially renowned.,,State Parks, Forests & Public Lands,The state maintains 35+ state parks, 9 state forests, wildlife management areas, and river trail systems, offering year round access to camping, cabins, swimming, boating, picnicking, and wildlife viewing. These public lands form the backbone of West Virginias outdoor lifestyle.,,Rivers, Fishing & Whitewater Rafting,,West Virginia is nationally recognized for its rivers and whitewater recreation, including the New River and Gauley River, which provide worldclass rafting, kayaking, and tubing. Anglers enjoy trout streams, bass rivers, and mountain lakes throughout the state.,,Rock Climbing & Adventure Sports,The New River Gorge National Park & Preserve, West Virginias only national park, offers over 1,400 established climbing routes, along with ziplining, bridge walks, and technical adventure activities. It is considered one of the premier climbing destinations in the eastern U.S.,,Hunting, Fishing & Wildlife Viewing,,West Virginias extensive public lands support big game and small game hunting, fishing access, and wildlife observation, including elk restoration areas, birding trails, and scenic backcountry habitat suitable for outdoor traditions and conservation minded land ownership.,,Four Season Recreation,Recreation continues year round with skiing, snowshoeing, cross country skiing, and winter hiking in higher elevations, while spring and summer highlight waterfalls, wildflowers, paddling, and camping.,,RECREATION APPEAL,Land near the New River supports a wide range of high demand outdoor uses:,,Whitewater rafting and paddling,Fly fishing and warmwater fishing,Hiking, biking, and backcountry access,Rock climbing and photography,Wildlife observation and hunting,The national park designation has increased visibility and value while ensuring the area remains intentionally rural.,,CLIMATE OVERVIEW,West Virginia has a moderate four season climate, shaped by its Appalachian Mountains and varied elevations. The result is comfortable summers, colorful falls, mild springs, and true winters without extreme heat or prolonged drought common in other regions.,,Spring (March-May),,Mild to cool temperatures with increasing sunshine,Wildflowers, blooming forests, and flowing streams,Ideal for planting, hiking, and fishing,Occasional rain helps keep the landscape lush,,Summer (June-August),,Warm but generally moderate, especially at higher elevations,Typical daytime highs range from the 70s to low 80sF in much of the state,Cooler nights in mountain and valley areas,Well suited for outdoor recreation like hiking, rafting, and camping,(West Virginia summers are notably less humid and cooler than much of the Southeast.),,Fall (September-November),,One of the states most celebrated seasons,Cool, dry air and low humidity,Brilliant fall foliage across mountains and forests,Excellent conditions for outdoor activities, hunting, and scenic travel,,Winter (December-February),,Cold but variable depending on elevation,Lower elevations: occasional snowfall, mixed with milder periods,Higher elevations: more consistent snow, supporting winter recreation,Winters are typically shorter and less severe than in the Northeast or Midwest,,Elevation Based Climate Variation,,Elevation ranges from river valleys to high ridges over 4,000 feet,Higher elevations: cooler summers, more snowfall,Valleys and lower areas: milder winters and slightly warmer summers,This variation creates microclimates ideal for diverse land uses, agriculture, and recreation,,Precipitation & Water,,Evenly distributed rainfall throughout the year,No pronounced dry season,Supports forests, streams, wildlife habitat, and reliable water resources,,,Why Buyers Like West Virginias Climate,,Comfortable four season living,No extreme heat waves or long droughts,Excellent for outdoor lifestyles and land stewardship,Predictable seasonal rhythm without coastal storm risk,DARK SKY EXPERIENCE IN WEST VIRGINIA,Why Dark Skies Matter,,Unobstructed star views and visible Milky Way,Quieter nights and preserved rural atmosphere,Ideal for retreats, eco tourism, off grid living, and astronomy,Enhances natural wildlife behavior and habitat health,Increasingly rare feature that adds ecological and lifestyle value,,West Virginia is widely recognized as one of the darkest states east of the Mississippi River, offering exceptional night sky visibility thanks to its rural character, mountainous terrain, and low population density. West Virginia offers some of the darkest night skies in the eastern U.S., with minimal light pollution and visible Milky Way views in many rural and mountain areas.,,Naturally Low Light Pollution,,With no large metropolitan areas and extensive forested land, much of West Virginia experiences minimal artificial light at night. In many regions, the night sky retains a deep natural darkness, allowing stars to appear in sharp detail and the Milky Way to be visible to the naked eye on clear nights.,,Certified Dark Sky Parks & Protected Areas,,West Virginia is home to International Dark Sky Park designations, including Watoga State Park, Calvin Price State Forest, and Droop Mountain Battlefield State Park. These areas are officially recognized for exceptional night sky quality and active protection against light pollution.,,OVERVIEW OF THE NEW RIVER,,Why the New River Matters Today,,Today, the New River represents clean water, outdoor adventure, preserved landscapes, and quiet rural living. Its designation as a national park has drawn renewed attention while maintaining the regions natural character, making the area attractive for conservation minded residents, landowners, and visitors seeking authentic Appalachian scenery.,,The New River is one of the oldest rivers in North America and possibly the world flowing northward through the Appalachian Mountains of North Carolina, Virginia, and West Virginia. Carved over millions of years, it has shaped dramatic gorges, fertile valleys, and some of the most scenic and ecologically rich landscapes in the eastern United States.,,Unlike most rivers in the region, the New River flows from south to north, beginning in the Blue Ridge Mountains of North Carolina, passing through southwest Virginia, and entering West Virginia before joining the Kanawha River near Gauley Bridge.,,Why the New River Area Works for Land Buyers,,National park proximity without urban congestion,Protected landscapes supporting long-term value,Strong recreation and lifestyle demand,Low population density and minimal light pollution,Accessible to airports, highways, and services,The New River region offers a rare alignment of conservation, accessibility, and lifestyle quality ideal for buyers seeking land with both intrinsic value and future stability.,,Recreation & Outdoor Significance,,The New River is internationally known for whitewater rafting, kayaking, and fishing. Different stretches of the river offer everything from calm, family friendly floats to technically challenging rapids. Its long, scenic paddling corridors also support camping, swimming, and wildlife observation,,In addition to water recreation, the New River Gorge is a major destination for rock climbing, hiking, mountain biking, and photography, with hundreds of miles of nearby trails and cliffs rising directly from the riverbanks.,,Ecology & Natural Importance,,The New River supports a remarkably diverse ecosystem, including rare plants, freshwater mussels, fish species, birds of prey, and forest wildlife. Its ancient origins and varied geology have created habitats not found elsewhere in the region.,,Because much of the river corridor remains undeveloped, it also serves as an important conservation and migration pathway through the Appalachian Mountains.,,________________________________________,, Cultural & Historical Role,,For generations, the New River has been central to Appalachian life, supporting Indigenous peoples, early settlers, farming communities, and later the coal and railroad industries. Abandoned rail towns, bridges, and historic structures still trace the rivers path, giving the region a deep sense of place and heritage.,,The iconic New River Gorge Bridge, one of the longest steel arch bridges in the Western Hemisphere, spans the gorge and has become a symbol of both engineering achievement and the regions connection between past and present.,,________________________________________,,Why the New River Matters Today,,Today, the New River represents clean water, outdoor adventure, preserved landscapes, and quiet rural living. Its designation as a national park has drawn renewed attention while maintaining the regions natural character, making the area attractive for conservation minded residents, landowners, and visitors seeking authentic Appalachian scenery.,,________________________________________,,Why the New River Area Works for Land Buyers,,National park proximity without urban congestion,Protected landscapes supporting long-term value,Strong recreation and lifestyle demand,Low population density and minimal light pollution,Accessible to airports, highways, and services,The New River region offers a rare alignment of conservation, accessibility, and lifestyle quality, ideal for buyers seeking land with both intrinsic value and future stability.,,New River Gorge & National Park,In southern West Virginia, the river cuts through a deep sandstone canyon known as the New River Gorge, now protected as the New River Gorge National Park and Preserve, West Virginia's only national park. Towering cliffs, forested slopes, and expansive overlooks make the gorge one of the most visually striking river corridors in the eastern U.S.,,The park protects more than 70,000 acres of land and river, preserving both natural ecosystems and historic coal mining communities that once relied on the river and surrounding rail lines.,,HATFIELD-MCCOY TRAILS,The Hatfield-McCoy Trails System (HMTS) is made up of over 700+ miles of trails and located in the rich mountains of southern West Virginia. The 700+ mile HMTS is second only to the 2000 mile long Paiute ATV Trail in Central Utah.,,As one of the largest off-highway vehicle trail systems in the world, HMTS is open 365 days a year and offers something for every skill level. The trail system caters to ATV, UATV, and motorbikes (dirt bikes), but hikers, mountain bikers, and horse riders can also use the trails. The trail system is a multi-county project, including West Virginia counties Logan, Kanawha, Wyoming, McDowell, Mercer, Wayne, Lincoln, Mingo, and Boone.,,The name of the trail system is derived from the names of two families, the Hatfields and McCoys, who famously feuded near the West Virginia and Kentucky border after the Civil War.,,Law enforcement officers patrol the trail to assure compliance with safety regulations. Motorized users of the trail system must wear a DOT-approved helmet and are prohibited from doubling (having a passenger), unless their vehicle is designed for two people. These rules, and a host of others, have allowed the trail system to enjoy a quality safety record, despite an increase in ATV-related injuries around the country.,,WEST VIRGINIA - A BRIEF OVERVIEW,Nickname: The Mountain State,Statehood: 1863; 35th state,Population 2025: 1,770,071,Capital: Charleston,Biggest City: Charleston 47,000 residents,Abbreviation: WV,State bird: Cardinal,State flower: Rhododendron,State Animal: Black Bear,The most forested state,,HISTORY,,After archaeologists discovered spear points used to hunt extinct species such as mastodons and mammoths, they realized that people have lived in what's now West Virginia for at least 10,500 years. Many thousands of years after these ancient people lived, Native American tribes including the Cherokee, Iroquois, Manahoac, Meherrin, Monacan, Nottaway, Shawnee, Occaneechi, Tutelo, and Saponi populated the land.,,After the British arrived in the 1600s, the area that now encompasses West Virginia, Virginia, Kentucky, and parts of North Carolina, Delaware, Pennsylvania, and New York was all called Virginia. In 1730, Virginias British-controlled government offered a thousand acres free to each European family willing to move to the area that would become West Virginia. As a result, Native Americans homelands were taken, and tribes began supporting the French in a land war against the British (often called the French and Indian War) from 1756 until 1763.,,The British won that battle, so West Virginia was still part of Virginia during the Revolutionary War of 1775 to 1783. But at the beginning of the Civil War (1861-1865), West Virginia refused to secede (withdraw) from the Union along with the rest of the state. John Brown, an abolitionist, someone who wanted to abolish slavery, staged a famous raid on Harpers Ferry in 1859. Brown hoped weapons gained in the raid would be used in the fight against slavery, but his raid failed. West Virginia separated from Virginia in 1861, and two years later, it became its own state.,,WHY IS IT CALLED THE MOUNTAIN STATE?,,West Virginia was originally going to be called Kanawha, a name that honors a Native American tribe. However, even though the region separated from Virginia, officials still wanted that as part of its new name. (Virginia was named after a nickname of Queen Elizabeth I, who ruled in the late 1500s.),,West Virginia is called the Mountain State because it is the only state completely within the Appalachian Mountain region, and its average elevation is higher than any other state east of the Mississippi River!,,GEOGRAPHY AND LANDFORMS,,Some people think this states shape looks like a leaping frog, with its nose in the southwestern corner. WV is bordered by Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Maryland in the north; Maryland and Virginia in the east; Virginia and Kentucky in the south; and Kentucky and Ohio in the west. The Ohio River creates its wiggly western border, while its winding eastern border is created by the Appalachian Mountains. It can be divided into two geographical regions.,,The Appalachian Ridge and Valley Region includes the Appalachian and Blue Ridge Mountains, which start in the northeast and run southwest. This region is known for its parallel ridges that were cut by streams, as well as canyons called water gaps. Forests, caves, and high peaks dot this area, including the states highest point, Spruce Knob.,,The Allegheny Plateau spreads across the rest of the state and has flat-topped hills and rounded peaks. Deep, stream-cut gorges and a wall of mountains called the Allegheny Front separate the states two regions.,,WILDLIFE,,At least seventy kinds of mammals inhabit West Virginia, including Virginia big-eared bats, West Virginia northern flying squirrels, raccoons, skunks, and black bears, the state animal. Wild turkeys, ruffed grouse, barred owls, bald eagles, cerulean warblers, and ruby-throated hummingbirds are among the three hundred species of birds that live in the state.,,Fence lizards, stinkpots (a kind of turtle), rattlesnakes, and five-lined skinks are some of the reptiles that slither and skitter through West Virginia. Amphibians such as tiny cricket frogs, mountain chorus frogs (Spring peepers), Allegheny Mountain dusky salamanders, newts, and West Virginia spring salamanders also live throughout the state.,,Some of West Virginias most common trees include oaks, poplar, hickory, maples, Black Walnut, and hemlock. The state also has many native wildflowers such as Black-Eyed Susans, Joe Pie Weed, bluebells, buttonweed, Virginia potato (which has edible roots), and wild strawberry.,,NATURAL RESOURCES,As the United States third most-forested state, West Virginia is known as a Resource State for its coal, timber, natural gas, quarry stone, rivers, and protected woodlands. It is also famous for its salt: Wild buffalo and deer gathered to lick natural salt deposits, and Native Americans and colonists gathered salt to cure butter and preserve meats. Today salt deposits are still mined for rock salt, which is then used to create chemicals such as chlorine.,,Coal, oil, timber, and natural gas, chemicals, and tourism are major contributors to the state's economy.

listings.description_full: NEW PRICE - $15,000 PRICE IMPROVEMENT!!,OVERVIEW,Turkey Creek Forest is a hidden gem in the beautiful mountains of Wild Wonderful West Virginia.  Along beautiful Turkey Creek lies this 82 +/- acre wooded property, with trails for ATV riding, beautiful mountain vistas and amazing home or cabin sites. Suited for the forever home or cabin for a recreational getaway, you dont want to miss this opportunity for privacy and seclusion, in the mountains of West Virginia.,,HIGHLIGHTS,Located on the waters of Turkey Creek,A nice mix of terrain,82 +/- acres by deed and surveys,Excellent hunting and wildlife viewing,Tremendous opportunity for cabins or dream homes,ATV, UTV the entire property,Historic Union is only a 15-minute drive,No deed restrictions,Low property taxes,,LOCATION,Google Coordinates: 37.538344(N), -80.550056(W),Address: Willow Bend Road, Union, WV 24983; No 911 address is assigned to property without structures.,Elevation Range: 1847 ft. to 2459 ft. +/-,,Driving Times (approximate),,Towns:,Union: 15 minutes,Peterstown: 35 minutes,Alderson: 45 minutes,Lewisburg and Osteopathic School of Medicine: 55 minutes,Princeton: 55 minutes,Athens and Concord University: 1 hour,Blacksburg, VA and Virginia Tech: 1 hour 10 minutes,Bluefield: 1 hour 10 minutes,,Airports:,Greenbrier Valley Airport, Lewisburg: 1 hour,Mercer County Airport, Bluefield: 1 hour 10 minutes,Raleigh County Memorial Airport, Beckley: 1 hour 30 minutes,Virginia Tech Montgomery Executive Airport, Blacksburg, VA: 1 hour 15 minutes,,Recreation:,Golf - Fountain Springs Golf Course: 30 minutes,Golf - Pipestem Resort State Park: 1 hour 15 minutes,Golf - Willow Wood Country Club Golf Course: 50 minutes,Lake - Bluestone Lake, Hinton: 1 hour,Lake - Moncove Lake State Park, Gap Mills: 35 minutes,Nature Trail - Mill Creek Nature Park Trails, Narrows, VA: 50 minutes,Skiing - Winterplace Ski Resort, Ghent: 1 hour 10 minutes,State Fair of West Virginia, Fairlea: 50 minutes,State Park - Camp Creek State Park & Forest: 1 hour 10 minutes,State Park - Bluestone State Park, Hinton: 1 hour,State Park - Moncove Lake State Park, Gap Mills: 35 minutes,State Park - Pipestem Resort State Park, Pipestem: 1 hour 15 minutes,,TIMBER / FOREST RESOURCES,The timber at Turkey Creek Forest adds a great deal of value to this property.  The abundant hardwood timber resource is a composite of high-quality Appalachian Hardwoods. This beautiful property was last select harvested about 30 years ago.  This well-maintained timber resource can provide a great deal of flexibility to the next ownership. Capital timber value of the timber and pulpwood has not yet been determined at this time. The forest has predominantly well-drained upland terrain which has led to a resource dominated by hardwood species. Overall, the species compensation is highly desirable and favors Appalachian hardwood types, consisting primarily of black walnut, sugar maple, Poplar, Basswood, Red Oak groups, White Oak and Chestnut Oak, Soft Maple, Hickory, and a host of associated species.,,WILDLIFE,Turkey Creek Forest has an abundant wildlife population, including turkey, bear, and whitetail deer.  The wild population is particularly impressive. The mixture of mature forest and emerging forest, and old farm fields, coupled with an abundant water supply, create the perfect wildlife habitat.,,The hardwood forest produced tons of acorns, hickory nuts, beechnuts and black walnut. Whitetail deer, wild turkey, squirrels, raccoons, fox and many species of songbirds and raptors make up the resident wildlife population.,,Turkey Creek both fosters aquatic plant life and creates a water-supported community with a wide variety of wildlife. The plant life associated with the creek area includes rushes, sedges, cattails, duckweed, and algae.,,It is hard to find a property that has a better mix of wildlife as there has been wildlife management practices in place for many years.,,HUNTERS PARADISE,Turkey Creek Forest is an awesome hunters' paradise and a great recreational property.  The property is surrounded by farm and corn fields which are the stuff that lead to the hunters' dream spot.  The property shares a common border with Turkey Creek, and with the abundance of Hickory White Oak, Red Oak, a habitat is created for large and small game.,,The year-round water source of Turkey Creek and the surrounding aquatic plant life create a water supported community with a wide variety of wildlife. Some of the margin of the creek supporting the aquatic food web, provide shelter for wildlife, and stabilize the shores of the stream. There are many animals that live in the water and around the edge of the spring fed creek including raccoons, possums, Blue Heron, turtles, salamanders, crayfish, bullfrog, Hawks and Red Wing Birds. The property has a mixture of hardwood species.  The Edge effect created between the creeks, hollows, ridges, rock out-croppings, and forest are textbook habitat benefiting all of the resident wildlife.,,The hardwood forest provides an essential nutrients source and produces tons of hardwood mask including acorns, hickory nuts, beechnut, and black walnut. Soft Mass includes sage horn, black cherry, tulip poplar seeds, maple seeds, autumn olive berries and blackberries.,,Whitetail deer, black bear, wild turkey, squirrels, rabbits, bobcats, raccoons, fox and many species of song birds and raptors makeup the resident wildlife population.,,WATER RESOURCES,Turkey Creek, a blueline stream, runs along a portion of the northeastern property boundary. The creek should have regular water flow, especially during periods of rainfall and snow melt.,,MINERAL RESOURCES,West Virginia is one of the states in the US that has two ownership titles, those being SURFACE RIGHTS and MINERAL RIGHTS. A title search for mineral rights ownership has not been conducted. All rights the owner has will convey with the property. listings.description_full: Discover an exceptionally clean, well-organized, and impressively equipped 29.92-acre farmstead at W3905 Highway 64 in Marinette, Wisconsin. Conveniently located approximately eight miles west of Marinette and five miles northwest of Peshtigo, this remarkable property combines a spacious single-family residence with extensive agricultural infrastructure suitable for livestock, grain handling, equipment storage, shop use, and a variety of farming operations.,,The well-kept residence offers four bedrooms and two-and-one-half bathrooms, along with a comfortable living room, dining room, bonus room, walk-in pantry, laundry room, and practical mudroom. Additional features include a full unfinished basement and radiant hydronic heating with a combination of in-floor and baseboard heat. The home’s generous room arrangement provides comfortable everyday living with the flexibility needed for a busy farm household.,,Surrounding the residence is an outstanding collection of 12 barns, shops, storage buildings, and agricultural structures. Highlights include a substantial 60' x 120' heated shop and cold-storage building, a 54' x 80' building with power and water, several additional powered buildings, multiple livestock barns equipped with automatic feeders and waterers, southern-exposure housing, and a 50' x 145' building with a concrete loading chute. The largest structure measures approximately 60' x 320' and includes four-foot concrete walls through a substantial portion of the building.,,The property also features an extensive grain-handling system with approximately 145,000 bushels of stated storage capacity across three aerated grain bins. The bins are equipped with fans, grain sweeps, load-out augers, and drying components. Supporting infrastructure includes a 75-foot grain leg rated at 3,000 bushels per hour, a 250-bushel dump pit, and a continuous dryer—providing the infrastructure expected of a fully operational agricultural property.,,Aerial views showcase an orderly and efficient farm layout with attractive open acreage, established access drives, ample maneuvering space, and thoughtfully positioned buildings. The residence, landscaped grounds, grain system, barns, and outbuildings collectively present an exceptionally clean and versatile agricultural setting.,,Whether your plans involve livestock production, grain storage and handling, equipment maintenance, agricultural storage, or a diversified farming enterprise, this wonderful Marinette County property offers the scale, infrastructure, and flexibility to support a wide range of agricultural uses—all centered around a comfortable family home.

listings.title: Old Sundance Ranch
listings.types_label: Farms and Ranches, Recreational Property, Hunting Property, House
listings.description_short: A proven Wyoming cattle and hunting ranch featuring strong grazing resources, abundant water, quality improvements, and exceptional opportunities for elk, deer, pronghorn, turkey, waterfowl, and upland birds.
listings.description_full: Old Sundance Ranch is a high-quality Wyoming cattle and hunting ranch near Sundance, built for serious cow/calf production with strong grass, abundant water, and functional improvements. The property offers excellent hunting for elk, mule deer, white-tailed deer, pronghorn, turkey, waterfowl and upland birds, combining dependable cattle performance with consistent big game opportunity.,,General Operations ,,Cattle,Old Sundance Ranch is first and foremost a proven cattle operation. The ranch is rated to support approximately 1,250 cow/calf pairs year-round, backed by a combination of native range and productive hay ground along the creek bottoms. These meadows have historically produced quality forage, supporting both winter feed and overall carrying capacity. The ranch is well-fenced and cross-fenced, with a layout that allows cattle to be moved, rotated, and managed efficiently. An extensive internal road system provides reliable access across the property, making day-to-day operations straightforward at this level.,Water,Water is one of the strongest attributes of the ranch and a key reason for its performance. The property is very well watered, with a combination of live water creeks, reservoirs, large mitigation ponds, springs, and developed water systems. Several creeks provide year-round flow, while others extend moisture through different seasons. In addition, wells and pipeline systems distribute water across the ranch, ensuring consistent availability for livestock in all areas. This level of water development supports both production and overall grazing efficiency.,Land,The ranch stretches from timbered ridges and draws on the eastern end into open native grass country to the west. This transition creates a highly usable landscape, with pine-covered ridges, protected bottoms, and broad grazing country. The ground is set up to be worked efficiently, with natural protection, consistent forage, and access throughout, allowing the ranch to be operated without compromise.,Hunting,While the ranch stands on its cattle operation alone, the hunting is equally compelling. The combination of timber, open country, and abundant water creates habitat that consistently holds and supports wildlife throughout the year. The ranch supports a resident herd of elk, with additional migratory elk moving through during the fall and winter, providing consistent opportunities at mature, quality bulls. Mule deer and white-tailed deer are both well established across the ranch, with the mix of cover, feed, and water producing solid populations and the potential for large, mature bucks.,Pronghorn are spread across the open grass country in strong numbers, taking advantage of the visibility and forage that the western portion of the ranch provides. Merriam’s turkeys are present in high densities throughout the ranch, particularly along the timbered ridges and creek bottoms, offering consistent hunting opportunity. The ranch’s extensive water--creeks, ponds, and reservoirs--draws significant numbers of waterfowl, especially in the early season, creating another layer of hunting value.,In addition to big game, upland birds are present on the ranch, including sharptailed grouse, found across the native grasslands and transitional areas. The diversity of terrain and the availability of water allow multiple species to utilize the same areas, and it is common to encounter elk, deer, antelope, and turkeys in close proximity. Overall, the ranch offers a consistent hunting experience, with the habitat and water necessary to support both quality animals and strong populations year after year.,Improvements,Improvements across Old Sundance Ranch are centered on supporting a large-scale cattle operation and are built with function and efficiency in mind. The working facilities are well maintained and designed to allow for efficient gathering and handling of livestock, with their placement and the ranch’s internal road system providing easy access and minimizing time and labor when moving cattle across the property. Fencing and cross-fencing are in place and support effective livestock management and rotation. The headquarters area includes multiple residences and supporting outbuildings that accommodate ranch operations and personnel, along with barns, shops, and other livestock-related structures that provide the infrastructure necessary to operate at this level with durability and ease of use.,Location,The ranch is located in a strong part of northeastern Wyoming, offering both access and proximity to key amenities. Sundance and Moorcroft provide local services, while Gillette offers a full range of commercial, medical, and regional amenities within a reasonable drive. Keyhole Reservoir is nearby and is a well-known destination for fishing, boating, and additional outdoor use. Air access is available via Gillette-Campbell County Airport (approximately 36 miles), Rapid City Regional Airport (approximately 78 miles), and Hulett Municipal Airport (approximately 25 miles). Access to the ranch is straightforward via county roads and nearby interstate connections, allowing for ease of travel without giving up the setting.
highlights: Rated to support approximately 1,250 cow/calf pairs year-round with productive hay meadows and native range
Extensive water resources including creeks, reservoirs, ponds, springs, wells, and developed pipeline systems
Exceptional hunting for elk, mule deer, whitetail deer, pronghorn, turkey, waterfowl, and upland birds
Functional headquarters, livestock facilities, fencing, cross-fencing, and road systems built for efficiency

listings.description_full: Located approximately 8 miles west of Kaycee, Wyoming, on the tree lined banks of the North Fork of the Powder River and nestled at the base of Wyoming’s majestic Bighorn Mountains, Pass Creek Ranch encompasses a striking diversity of landscapes that combine both agricultural productivity and exceptional recreational appeal. The ranch consists of 4,389± total acres, comprises of 3,231± deeded acres, 680± State of Wyoming lease acres and 478± BLM acres. A defining feature of the Ranch is its abundance of live water and valuable water rights. Pass Creek Ranch benefits from extensive water rights including territorial rights from the North Fork of the Powder River as well as rights from Pass Creek and the Dull Knife Reservoir system, supporting approximately 473± pivot and 85± flood irrigated acres of hay ground which are enhanced by the four center pivots. The City of Kaycee supplies the headquarters and an extensive water line system that includes a 10,000-gallon storage tank and approximately 10 tire tanks for domestic and stock water. The headquarters feature a 3-bed, 2-bath home built in 2017 that has many upgrades. In addition, there is a 1,200 sq. ft manufactured home built in 1970, two sets of corrals, and support buildings typical for the ranching operation. Historically, the ranch has supported approximately 175 cow/calf pairs on a year-round basis. Located in Hunt Area 34, the ranch is situated in a region known for supporting some of the largest elk herds in eastern Wyoming. Additional wildlife commonly found on the property includes antelope, wild turkey, coyotes, upland game birds, and occasional mountain lions. From the banks of the Pass Creek Reservoir or the meadows on the river bottoms or the vistas of the pasture land there are sweeping views of the Bighorn Mountains which serve as a dramatic backdrop throughout the property.
highlights: Extensive water rights and abundant live water resources throughout the property.

listings.description_short: Luxury Wyoming estate on 14.5 acres with direct national forest boundary, elevated setting, permanent mountain views, & professional-grade stewardship. Includes custom lodge residence (~5,100 SF) furnished guest cabin (~900 SF) heated 6-car garage (~1,775 SF) & firewood storage. Horse-zoned, fully fenced, gated access.
listings.description_full: This unique and stunning property is situated on 14.5 acres zoned for horses. The house is located in a world-class snowmobiling, hunting, and fishing area, and this home can accommodate groups of people for such activities and has plenty of room to park trailers and equipment as well as entertain your guests. It commands a panoramic 360-degree view of the Wyoming Range and Wind River Range. Watch breathtaking sunsets on the back porch or in the hot tub, or watch sunrises on the front porch over the Wind River Mountains. The property has 3 buildings consisting of the main house at 5100 sq. ft., a 6-car garage at 1775 sq. ft., and a guest cabin at 900 sq. ft.,,This home is perfect for skiers, snowmobilers, hunters, and fishermen. This home gives you the option of participating in any, all, or none of these activities but to come home to a true lodge atmosphere.,It is a custom architect-designed log home with glue-laminated beams to add to the western log home atmosphere. ,,Home is located 70 miles south of Jackson Hole, Wyoming. Sublette County is in the heart of world-class trout fishing along the many streams and rivers coming out of the Wyoming Range or Wind River Range. This home is riding distance to the Bridger Teton National Forest at the end of Fayette Pole Creek Road, providing the best opportunities in Wyoming for snow machining, hiking, horseback riding, four-wheeling, and world-class elk, moose, mule deer, pronghorn, and mountain sheep hunting. The local ski lodge and lift fulfill any skier's desire, whether expert or beginner. Day trips to Yellowstone National Park provide one of the best opportunities to experience a true national park. ,,Sublette County School District is one of the richest in the State of Wyoming, having access to the best facilities. Low student-teacher ratios, along with a hometown atmosphere and modern computer-aided facilities, provide the growing student with an excellent learning atmosphere. The complete world-class aquatic center with a climbing wall, running track, Olympic swimming pool, and inside water park provides a one-of-a-kind unique experience open to the public and used by the students.,,Elevated above the surrounding landscape, the property commands unobstructed 360-degree views of both the Wyoming Range and the Wind River Range. This rare dual-range vantage point is effectively impossible to recreate under current zoning, environmental, and land-use regulations. These protected viewsheds are not simply scenic. They represent permanence in a market increasingly defined by encroachment, fragmentation, and visual dilution, ensuring what is seen today remains unchanged for generations.,,The estate’s architectural lodge residence, guest cabin, garage, and supporting infrastructure were intentionally sited to maximize elevation, privacy, solar exposure, and sightlines. These decisions would be exceedingly difficult, if not impossible, to duplicate today. Direct national forest adjacency, coupled with horse zoning and low-density surroundings, ensures long-term insulation from development pressure while preserving access to wildlife corridors and four-season recreation.,,Elk, moose, mule deer, pronghorn, and bighorn sheep move through the adjoining land as they have for generations, reinforcing the sense that this is not merely a property but part of a larger, intact ecosystem.,,Located approximately 70 miles south of Jackson Hole in Sublette County, the estate benefits from proximity to world-class recreation without exposure to resort density, congestion, or transient development cycles. This balance of access without overexposure is increasingly rare in the Mountain West and central to the property’s long-term desirability.,,In today’s market, replacement cost has become a misleading metric. The true constraint is not expense, but impossibility. Comparable land positions offering direct national forest boundaries, elevated terrain, protected views, and established infrastructure are finite and steadily disappearing. Once lost, they cannot be recreated at any price.,,This offering represents a finite asset class, a generational holding defined by land position rather than improvements, by access rather than excess, and by permanence rather than trend. It is a property intended not merely to be owned but to be stewarded, one of the last remaining opportunities to secure scale, privacy, and authenticity in a landscape where those qualities are no longer being produced.,,Together, these characteristics establish a level of scarcity that transcends market cycles and stylistic preferences. The land itself is the luxury, carrying intrinsic value rooted in geography, protection, and time. As development pressures continue across the Mountain West, opportunities of this scale and integrity become increasingly constrained, reinforcing the estate’s position as a long-term store of value, a private refuge, and a legacy holding capable of serving multiple generations without compromise. Its significance lies not in trend or timing but in permanence, restraint, and stewardship, qualities that increasingly define the highest tier of land ownership in the modern West for discerning owners seeking authenticity, longevity, and meaning.

Elevated 14.5 acres with unobstructed 360° mountain views
Custom lodge, guest cabin, and heated 6-car garage compound

listings.description_full: Echo Mountain Ranch is located where the historic town of Boxelder once thrived.  This 5,936+/- ranch is 45 minutes from Casper, Wyoming south of Glenrock, Wyoming.  Ranging from lush meadows to mountain peaks, this ranch has it all!  ,,This property falls in an opportunity zone...great for an investor!,,Land ,,As you enter the ranch, rolling meadows bisected by year around streams open to sub-irrigated valleys leading into the dark timber. Resident beavers control the water as it flows from the mountains creating dozens of ponds and excellent habitat for wildlife. The sod base is lush and thick allowing for excellent animal growth, both domestic and wild. Large rock outcropping line the canyon walls creating a very picturesque landscape. Historic cabins throughout the property have been remodeled to maintain the character of the past while providing shelter. Several fishing ponds are scattered throughout the ranch which are also frequented by waterfowl.,All of the hay meadows have been over-seeded and leveled to produce a more consistent stand of grass.  Alfalfa food plots are located in the transition zones to help pinpoint Elk activity. Two track roads are maintained to make traversing the 5,936 acres easy, whether in a side by side or vehicle.,Echo Mountain Ranch is very well watered. Irrigated ditches run late into fall and the main streams flow year around. Each valley has a tributary which catches spring runoff.  Dozens of ponds and manmade reservoirs are scattered throughout the entire ranch providing waterholes and habitat.,,,Improvements ,,Three homes just off the county road offer abundant living space. One is newly remodeled and updated and a second is in process now. Additional living quarters for a ranch hand is tied into one of the buildings. A historic barn has been restored as well as the horse stalls and riding arena. New metal buildings have been built to provide heated storage for all the equipment. The corrals and fencing have all been updated and are continually being improved. A private solar system has been installed and it has reduced the monthly cost of electricity drastically.,Vintage cabins have been restored to offer accommodations for one seeking to take in the outdoors and wildlife from the viewpoint of the time of the Pony Express.,,,Recreation ,,The recreational opportunities on this ranch are endless. Whether you like the outdoors or are an avid trophy hunter, you will not be disappointed. The elk herd on the property thrives, producing some of the largest bulls found in Wyoming. Restrictions set by Game and Fish to manage the herd has produced abundant 66 bulls. The pictures and videos do not do it justice!,Upland birds and mountain grouse are plentiful as the ecosystems created by the beaver ponds provide food, water and cover to support successful hatches each year.  Wild turkeys can be heard in every valley in between the elk bugles.,Antelope thrive on the plateau flats while finding shelter near the aspen groves. Quality mule deer and whitetail deer can be seen frequently and the herds seem to grow larger each year.,One wanting to take advantage of the migration, the waterfowl hunting is excellent.,,,Agriculture ,,The hay meadows are being constantly improved through grading, leveling and seeding. The growth rate on the cattle is a testament of proof. If ones focus was on cattle, capacity would be one of the best in the area. Currently the mountain is left to stand to ensure ample food for the resident elk herd.,,,Location ,,Echo Mountain Ranch is approximately a 45 minute drive to Casper, Wyoming. Glenrock is less than 20 minutes away.

listings.types_label: Farms and Ranches, Commercial Property, House
listings.description_short: Luxury estate featuring a lodge-style residence, event venue, productive farmland, managed wildlife habitat, and turnkey recreational amenities in Middle Tennessee.
listings.description_full: King B Farm presents a distinctive opportunity to acquire an approximately 675-acre mixed-use estate in southern Middle Tennessee. Located minutes from I-65, the property combines productive agricultural land, professionally managed wildlife habitat, a turnkey sporting operation, an established event campus and approximately 25,000 square feet of residential, hospitality, event and agricultural buildings.,,The approximately 7,500-square-foot main residence has been extensively renovated and expanded into a refined lodge-style retreat featuring two full kitchens, generous gathering spaces, a dramatic trophy room, expansive primary suite, finished lower level, smart-home technology, outdoor entertaining areas and a custom black walnut gun vault. Additional accommodations include the Bethany Bridal Cottage and a separate accessible guest residence known as the Groom’s House.,,The developed event campus centers around a restored historic horse barn transformed into an elegant ballroom while retaining elements of its original equestrian architecture. Venue improvements include a landscaped ceremony garden overlooking Indian Creek, commercial catering kitchen, spacious restrooms, high-speed Starlink internet, security systems and professionally maintained grounds. The venue has successfully accommodated events ranging from intimate gatherings to celebrations exceeding 200 guests. Although event operations are not currently active, the physical improvements, branding, vendor relationships, event equipment and specified FF&E remain in place, offering a substantial foundation for future reactivation or repositioning, subject to applicable approvals.,,Approximately 110 acres are currently used for agricultural production, while roughly 500 acres have been maintained as low-disturbance wildlife habitat. More than fifteen years of informed management have established the property as a turnkey sporting estate with mature whitetail habitat, improving wild turkey populations, seven enclosed shooting blinds, additional ladder stands, feeding and trail-camera areas, and an extensive internal ATV and utility-vehicle trail system. Event and recreational equipment included in the sale will be identified on a separate inventory.,,The estate also carries more than two centuries of regional history. Historic features include the original 1903 King residence, Goode-Ordway Cemetery, surviving agricultural structures and a limestone wall extending more than half a mile along King Road.,,With access to Huntsville International Airport approximately 34 miles away and Nashville International Airport approximately 88 miles away, King B Farm is positioned for continued use as a private estate, luxury event destination, executive retreat, sporting lodge, corporate compound, agricultural operation or multi-use hospitality property.,,Investment highlights,• ±675-Acre Mixed-Use Estate,,• ±25,000 SF Across All Structures,,• ±7,500 SF Lodge-Style Main Residence,,• Established Event Venue | Up to 299 Guests,,• ±110 Acres in Agricultural Production,,• ±500 Acres of Managed Wildlife Habitat,,• Turnkey Sporting Infrastructure Included,,• Event Equipment and Specified FF&E Included,,• Minutes to I-65 | ±34 Miles to HSV | ±88 Miles to BNA

Restored event venue featuring ballroom, ceremony garden, catering kitchen, and capacity for large gatherings
Managed wildlife habitat with mature deer hunting, turkey populations, shooting blinds, and extensive trail system
Strategic location near I-65 with access to Huntsville and Nashville airports for regional and national travel

agents.about: For over 40 years, Ive helped Texans buy, sell, and shape ranch land with a clear understanding of what makes each property truly valuable. I know the terrain, the water, the access, and the stories behind the land. My work centers on connecting the right people with the right acreage and guiding every step with honesty and experience. If youre looking to move land or find your next ranch, Im here to make it straightforward.

agents.name: Jeff Burleson
agents.about: The outdoors runs deep within the roots of this Carolina outdoor enthusiast. As a young boy, Jeff Burleson trampled the woods after a deer or duck and paddled the waters for a limit of fish alongside his father, two older brothers, and one younger brother in Robeson County. Burleson's love for nature and the outdoors fueled his outdoor hobbies and directed his studies towards a Bachelor's of Science degree in Fisheries and Wildlife Sciences in 1996 from N.C. State University. Since college, Burleson has held several positions with a variety of government and private entities practicing land sales, forestry, wetland consulting, wildlife management, endangered species consulting, and other natural resources duties. Burleson is a professional realtor and broker in both North and South Carolina with more than 10 years of land sales experience.

agents.name: Anna Renfro
agents.company: East Texas Ranch & Rec Land Realty, LLC

agents.name: Nick Wells
agents.about: Nicholas “Nick” Wells is Vice President and Designated/Managing Broker of American Legacy Land Company. With more than 12 years of land sales experience, Nick specializes in large farms, ranches, recreational properties, hunting land, and complex real estate transactions throughout Southwestern Nebraska, Eastern Colorado, and Northwestern Kansas.

agents.name: Collier Jones
agents.about: I, Collier Jones - Broker of Triple C Real Estate, LLC, am committed, conscientious, and caring. My specialized knowledge of the Texas Hill Country coupled with my exceptional customer service makes me the credible Broker you want to represent you in buying or selling property.

agents.name: Zeb White
agents.about: Zeb is the proud fifth-generation resident of rural Utah, where he has spent the majority of his life. Throughout his upbringing, Zeb actively participated in a variety of land projects, collaborating with his family on endeavors for farmers, ranchers, the Bureau of Land Management, various state agencies, and the US Forest Service. These formative years instilled in him a strong work ethic and a deep understanding of land management for diverse purposes. Zeb's exposure to this world fostered a profound appreciation for the great outdoors and ignited his passion for fishing, hunting, hiking, and exploring the natural beauty of Utah and beyond.

agents.name: J MARIE
agents.about: JBYRDMGMT LLC is a New Yorkbased land acquisition, investment, and strategic advisory firm with a dual focus: delivering high-quality vacant land opportunities and driving measurable business outcomes for clients across industries.

agents.name: Jady Conboy
agents.about: My career blends entrepreneurship, leadership, and a deep understanding of market dynamics. Beyond work, my true passion is the outdoors. Living in Pennsylvania, I find inspiration in its landscapes—whether on horseback or exploring with my husband and daughters. As a real estate agent, I specialize in representing sellers of land, rural homes, farms, and custom high-end properties. I am recognized as an expert at positioning land for residential development where it’s ideally suited—helping property owners maximize value by aligning with the right builders and developers. This requires a deep understanding of zoning, infrastructure, and market demand, and I thrive on guiding clients through this complex but rewarding process. When development isn’t the best path, I help sellers of rural estates, farms, and custom homes connect with the right buyers who will appreciate the unique lifestyle, character, and long-term value of their property. My approach is always tailored, ensuring each property is represented with care, strategy, and precision to achieve the strongest possible outcome. At the heart of my work is helping property owners unlock the full potential of their land or home—whether through development or by finding the perfect buyer—so they can move forward with confidence and success.

agents.name: Max Wierda
agents.about: Having lived in Michigan my entire life, I've developed a genuine passion and in-depth knowledge of its real estate landscape. Specifically; hunting land, farms, country estates, waterfront, and recreational properties. Lets discuss why sellers and buyers put their trust and confidence in me with all their real estate needs and aspirations.

agents.name: Ted Villien
agents.about: We are dedicated to helping individuals and families achieve their dreams of land ownership with integrity, care, and a steadfast commitment to excellence. Rooted in a spirit of innovation and inspired by the enduring Texan legacy of land stewardship, we strive to empower every client on their journey to owning a piece of the land they can call their own.

agents.name: Eugene D. Ninnie, PE, AIA, LEED AP
Moose Pond Lodge
agents.about: As the proud owner of Moose Pond Lodge, Im offering this extraordinary property For Sale by Owner to give buyers a more personal and transparent experience. Youll be working directly with someone who knows every detail of the land, the lodge, and the lifestyle it offers.

agents.name: Tim Gangl, ALC
agents.about: Tim is a Minnesota Broker and an Associate Broker with Peoples Company. Tim has been selling land and agricultural properties in Minnesota since early 2020 as part of a farmland brokerage team with a 50-year history in land sales, land auctions, land management, and 1031 tax deferred exchanges throughout the country. In 2024, Tim joined Peoples Company and is enthusiastically moving forward in his journey in land brokerage and land auctions, and is excited to be an integral part of the Peoples Company Minnesota team.

agents.name: Mac Blink
agents.about: ABOUT LANDBATCH RURAL AMERICA

agents.name: Mark Harman
agents.about: Mark Harman is a trusted Broker Associate with Kuper Sothebys International Realty and a 13-year real estate veteran based in Fredericksburg, Texas, the epicenter of Texas Wine Country. Nestled in the heart of the Hill Country and home to over 100 wineries and vineyards, Fredericksburg offers an unmatched lifestyle that Mark expertly navigates for his clients. His specialties include luxury homes on acreage, live water recreational properties, hunting ranches, family retreats, and high-end residential real estate. With deep roots in the region and a passion for its lifestyle, Mark helps clients find their ideal oasis in the Hill Country.

agents.name: Christopher Buchanan
agents.about: Chris is a native of Georgia and enjoys a lifelong passion for the great outdoors. He credits his career to his passion for the outdoors. He has helped landowners achieve

agents.name: Paul Ellsworth
agents.about: At South Harpeth Land Company, we want you to find your dream property as much as you want to find it. That's because we walked in your shoes.

agents.name: Pedro Santos
agents.about: Santos Solutions Management, LLC is a New York-based land acquisition and investment company specializing in affordable vacant residential lots across Michigan, Pennsylvania, and select emerging markets. We focus on sourcing off-market parcels and preparing each property for a smooth transaction from contract to closing.

agents.name: Sam Fahl
agents.about: Acer Paradise Inc., which is our timber land holding company, has decided to sell their properties located in northern lower Michigan. These lands have been intensely managed over the last 4 decades and have provided tremendous rate of returns on timber harvests. We can provide the documentation on the recent timber harvests.

agents.name: Ryan Fitzhugh
agents.about: Ryan Fitzhugh

agents.name: Tom Sullivan
agents.about: Tom has a deep-rooted passion for selling land that exudes from any conversation with him about land and farms. As a Tennessee native, Tom is knowledgeable about every region of the State of Tennessee, with a focus on Middle Tennessee. His ten-year stint in the Plantation Belt of Albany, Georgia further instilled a love for the land and the allure of land ownership.
